CYTOGENETICS LABORATORY REPORT
[redacted location] Children's Hospital
Department of Clinical Genetics

PATIENT INFORMATION
Patient: [redacted name]
DOB: [redacted date]
MRN: [redacted ID]
Specimen Type: Peripheral blood
Date Collected: [redacted date]
Date Received: [redacted date]
Date Reported: [redacted date]

CLINICAL INDICATION
Newborn with clinical features suggestive of Down syndrome

TEST PERFORMED
Rapid aneuploidy screening by quantitative fluorescence PCR (QF-PCR)
Conventional cytogenetic analysis (G-banded karyotype)

PRELIMINARY RESULTS - RAPID PCR SCREENING
QF-PCR analysis targeting chromosomes 13, 18, 21, X and Y
Result: Trisomy 21 detected
Three distinct alleles identified for chromosome 21 markers
Normal disomic pattern for chromosomes 13, 18, X and Y

FINAL KARYOTYPE RESULT
46,XY,der(14;21)(q10;q10),+21

ABNORMAL MALE KARYOTYPE

TECHNICAL DESCRIPTION
G-banded chromosome analysis was performed on cultured peripheral blood lymphocytes. Twenty metaphase cells were analyzed at a resolution of 550 bands. The karyotype shows 46 chromosomes with a Robertsonian translocation between the long arms of chromosomes 14 and 21, resulting in a derivative chromosome der(14;21). An additional free chromosome 21 is present, resulting in functional trisomy 21.

The breakpoints occur at the centromeric regions (q10) of both chromosomes 14 and 21. The short arm material from both chromosomes is lost, which typically contains no essential genetic material.

INTERPRETATION
This karyotype confirms the diagnosis of Down syndrome (trisomy 21) in this newborn patient. The trisomy 21 results from the presence of a Robertsonian translocation between chromosomes 14 and 21, plus an additional free chromosome 21. This represents translocation trisomy 21, which accounts for approximately 3-4% of Down syndrome cases.

The clinical phenotype is expected to be indistinguishable from that of standard trisomy 21. However, the presence of a Robertsonian translocation has important implications for genetic counseling and recurrence risk assessment.

RECOMMENDATIONS
1. Parental blood samples are urgently needed for karyotype analysis to determine whether the Robertsonian translocation is inherited or de novo
2. If either parent carries the balanced translocation, there is an increased risk for future pregnancies
3. Genetic counseling should be provided after parental karyotyping results are available
4. Standard medical management for Down syndrome is indicated
5. Referral to pediatric genetics clinic for comprehensive evaluation and family counseling

Authorized by: [redacted name], PhD, FACMG
Laboratory Director
